text.p: The sale of adulterated products, including shampoo and toothpaste, by private entrepreneurs in Havana has become widespread, Cuba's weekly Juventud Rebelde reported on Sunday.

"A high percentage of products sold on the streets and at some free enterprise markets in Havana are adulterated by unscrupulous individuals that seek profits at the expense of the health of their clients," the newspaper said.

Small private businesses were legalised in 1993 when the government gave up its three decade-old monopoly on manufacturing, sales, repairs and public services in more than 150 sectors of the economy. Some 200,000 people have been issued licenses for small businesses, but are forbidden to hire help outside the immediate family.

Juventud Rebelde said that public health inspectors who analysed 1,500 products sold by the private entrepreneurs discovered that "shampoo, deodorant, toothpaste and other personal hygiene products contained a high proportion of foreign substances."
Many of the items use factory-made products as their base but are then altered in order to double or triple the amount.
The newspaper said police had confiscated raw materials from shoemakers and dressmakers that had been stolen or obtained illegally, sometimes through bribery, from state-owned stores or warehouses.
Police said that "diverting" state property illegally into the hands of individuals was made possible "by the negligence and lack of vigilance of the state-owned enterprises."
